title: Sashweights and Birdshot: On Equalizing Inequity
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Underwood uses Kurt Vonnegut's story 'Harrison Bergeron', in which graceful ballerinas are weighed down with sashweights, as a lens on the Science of Reading Act passed by the House in September 2026. He argues the bill does not mandate phonics for every child directly but attaches priority in a federal literacy grant to alignment with the science of reading and bans so-called three-cueing, ratifying the state phonics laws already in place. His central worry is that uniform phonics instruction adds weight for children who already decode well, slowing them without any harm a test would detect. He cites Connor and Morrison's randomized work on child-by-instruction interactions and the National Reading Panel's own limited findings to show that the effects of phonics depend on the child. He explains the policy blind spot as a matter of advocacy: struggling decoders have parents and organizations in the hearing room, while fluent readers do not. He also contends that legislators misdescribe Marie Clay's Reading Recovery, which he taught within, as anti-phonics.
points: The federal bill works by shifting grant priorities and ratifying state laws, so its force comes from the system of forty-plus state reading laws behind it.

Connor and Morrison's randomized studies found that children with weak word recognition gained from code-focused teaching while stronger readers gained more from meaning-focused teaching, so uniform instruction is not optimal.
The cost of drilling children who already read is lost time for books, conversation and writing, a harm that is real but invisible to standard tests.
Policy overlooked this risk because one harm has vivid advocates and a simple story, while the other has no organized constituency and a story that does not fit on a floor speech.
Underwood argues that the 'three-cueing' ban rests on a misreading of Marie Clay and Reading Recovery, which in his experience gave heavy attention to letters and sounds.
quotes: Nobody puts weights on children deliberately. The danger is a policy that adds weight without knowing it.

The bill asks states applying for that money to describe “the extent to which the State comprehensive literacy instruction plan is aligned to the science of reading.” It directs the Department of Education to give priority to aligned applications.
Their starting point was simple: the same instruction doesn’t have the same effect on every child.
Children did better when the type and amount of instruction matched what they brought with them.

A child who already reads, sitting through daily phonics drills built for a classmate who can’t, isn’t being harmed in a way that a test would detect. That child is being slowed down, losing valuable time that could have gone to reading books, to conversations about books, to writing, and to the kind of mentoring that builds readers.
I don’t think the bill’s sponsors weighed this risk and rejected it. I think they never saw it. A trade-off can’t be weighed if half of it is ignored.
There were no parents of fluent readers bored through phonics drills advocating for a more rational approach. Such children have no advocacy organization.
Organized advocacy had a route to the House hearing that unorganized opposition did not.
